item.title: Vietnam’s New Land Law Could Speed Up Priority Projects but Weaken Farmers’ Bargaining Power
item.description: Vietnam’s revised land law, effective July 2027, could speed up priority projects by allowing some land acquisition decisions before compensation plans are approved. The change could weaken farmers’ ...
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam’s New Land Law Could Speed Up Priority Projects but Weaken Farmers’ Bargaining Power Vietnam’s revised land law, effective July 2027, could speed up priority projects by allowing some land acquisition decisions before compensation plans are approved. The change could weaken farmers’ bargaining power, putting pressure on provincial authorities to value land fairly, resolve objections and pay households on time. Devdiscourse News Desk | Updated: 22-11-2026 13:53 IST | Created: 22-11-2026 13:53 IST

Representative Image.

Country:

Vietnam

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Vietnam's National Assembly approved a revised land law on November 21, giving authorities a faster route to acquire land for certain projects. The law generally takes effect on July 1, 2027, and was passed with 466 of 479 participating deputies voting in favour. For Vietnam, the potential gain is more predictable delivery of infrastructure and industrial projects. For farmers and other land users, the change raises a more immediate question: how much influence will they have over compensation once authorities can issue an acquisition decision before the payment plan is final?

Faster land clearance could give Vietnam more predictable project timelines Land disputes can delay projects when households challenge compensation offers they consider below market value. The revised law addresses one source of delay by changing the order of decisions. In eligible cases, authorities can issue a land acquisition decision before approving the compensation plan. An earlier National Assembly resolution already allowed accelerated land recovery in some circumstances, including for nationally important projects ordered to proceed faster and urgent public investment projects. The revised law builds on that approach.

For public agencies and developers, earlier decisions could make it easier to coordinate site preparation, construction contracts and financing. The economic gain depends on whether sites actually become available sooner. If disputes over valuation or payment carry over into later stages, the time saved on the acquisition decision could be offset by delays before construction begins.

Farmers could lose bargaining power before compensation is settled Farmland is especially exposed because a household can lose its source of income without having to move. Chris Luong, a partner at CNC Counsel, said the faster procedure could therefore matter more for agricultural plots than for residential property. For farmers, the practical questions are how long they can keep using their land, when compensation arrives and whether a replacement plot can sustain production.

Two consent rules matter here. The earlier implementing decree identifies a route to an acquisition decision before compensation approval when more than 75% of land users agree. Reporting on the adopted law describes a separate mechanism for recovering the remaining land in a negotiated project after an investor has secured agreements covering more than 75% of both the land area and the land users. The distinction matters to developers assembling a site and to households that remain in negotiations after most neighbours have agreed.

Provincial authorities face the hardest decisions on compensation Vietnam's government says the law gives priority to compensation in land with the same use as the land acquired. It also provides for other forms of compensation, including housing or cash, subject to the circumstances and what is available locally. That makes provincial capacity consequential. A same-use plot can help a farming household keep earning, while a cash award leaves the household to find replacement land or another source of income. The options will vary with local land supply.

Policymakers also face a timing issue. The law generally takes effect in July 2027, while the new land price schedules and adjustment coefficients are due to apply from January 1, 2028. For cases that span those dates, households and investors will need clarity on which valuation rules apply. Publishing the basis for each offer and the route for challenging it would help land users assess compensation and give developers a clearer view of likely costs.

The first cases will show whether faster decisions deliver fairer outcomes Hanoi's proposed $28 billion Red River redevelopment shows how much can turn on compensation. Bloomberg reported that about 280,000 people live in the area covered by the project and that city officials proposed higher payments amid resistance. The dispute illustrates the stakes when a project affects homes, livelihoods and neighbourhood ties at the same time. Whether any part of the project can use an accelerated procedure depends on the applicable acquisition and resettlement rules.

The first cases under the revised law should show how provinces record consent, handle objections and sequence possession and payment. For Vietnam, the measure of success is whether priority projects reach construction sooner. For affected households, it is whether they receive compensation and livelihood support in time to replace what they lose. Tracking both outcomes would show whether the reform resolves delays or shifts their cost onto land users.

item.title: "Going to be permanent": Trump on making a deal with Iran
item.description: US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that any potential agreement with Iran would be "permanent" and aimed at preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, reiterating his insistence on ...
item.content:encoded:
"Going to be permanent": Trump on making a deal with Iran US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that any potential agreement with Iran would be "permanent" and aimed at preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, reiterating his insistence on securing what he described as a genuine and lasting deal with the country. ANI | Updated: 21-11-2026 22:02 IST | Created: 21-11-2026 22:02 IST

US President Donald Trump (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that any potential agreement with Iran would be "permanent" and aimed at preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons, reiterating his insistence on securing what he described as a genuine and lasting deal with the country. "I'm going to make a deal that is going to be permanent. I’m not going to let somebody allow them to have a nuclear weapon," Trump said, expressing his determination to ensure that Iran does not develop nuclear weapons. In an interview with Fox News, Trump also said he had never been particularly interested in regime change in Iran while describing his attacks on the country's senior leadership as a significant shift for the Iranian regime. He characterised Iran's new leadership as "more rational", but questioned its reliability in negotiations, alleging that Tehran had a history of making agreements and subsequently breaking them. The latest remarks come amid continuing tensions between Washington and Tehran, with Trump repeatedly expressing dissatisfaction over the terms Iran has been willing to offer in negotiations. Earlier on Friday, following his visit to China, Trump launched a sharp criticism of Tehran, accusing Iran of misleading people for decades and insisting that any agreement with Washington must meet US expectations. Speaking at a press conference, the US President linked fluctuations in gasoline prices to the outcome of negotiations with Iran, arguing that Tehran wanted an agreement but had not offered terms acceptable to him. "The prices of gasoline now, that also depends on how we settle up with Iran. They want to make a deal, but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me. We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they've been doing for 51 years. No longer 47. People talk 47. It's 51 years," Trump said. Taking a further swipe at Tehran, Trump accused Iran of misleading people over the past five decades, remarking, "They've been bullsh***ing people for 51 years." Trump's latest comments underscore his continued push for an agreement that would prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, while maintaining that Washington would not accept a deal that falls short of its expectations. His remarks come amid continuing tensions in West Asia, with Washington weighing its options regarding Iran, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reportedly urged the US administration to consider renewed military action against Tehran. While Trump has indicated that he is seeking a lasting diplomatic agreement, his statements also reflect his continued criticism of Iran's negotiating approach and the terms offered by Tehran. (ANI)

item.title: 5.7-magnitude earthquake strikes China
item.description: An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 struck China at a depth of 80 kilometres on Saturday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, reporting another seismic event in the country earlier this month.
item.content:encoded:
5.7-magnitude earthquake strikes China An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 struck China at a depth of 80 kilometres on Saturday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, reporting another seismic event in the country earlier this month. ANI | Updated: 21-11-2026 17:18 IST | Created: 21-11-2026 17:18 IST

Representational Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 struck China at a depth of 80 kilometres on Saturday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, reporting another seismic event in the country earlier this month. According to the NCS, the earthquake occurred at 4:15:37 pm IST on November 21, at latitude 37.099° North and longitude 96.482° East, with its location reported in China. In a post on X, the National Center for Seismology stated, "EQ of M: 5.7, On: 21/11/2026 16:15:37 IST, Lat: 37.099 N, Long: 96.482 E, Depth: 80 Km, Location: China." The latest earthquake comes after a 4.4-magnitude tremor was recorded in China on November 5. The earlier earthquake occurred at 6:19:17 am IST at a shallow depth of 10 kilometres, with its epicentre at latitude 32.592° North and longitude 94.291° East, according to the NCS. In its post on X, the NCS reported, "EQ of M: 4.4, On: 05/11/2026 06:19:17 IST, Lat: 32.592 N, Long: 94.291 E, Depth: 10 Km, Location: China." The two earthquakes fall into different depth categories under the classification outlined by the United States Geological Survey (USGS). While the November 5 earthquake, at a depth of 10 kilometres, falls in the shallow category, the latest tremor, recorded at 80 kilometres, is classified as an intermediate-depth earthquake. According to the USGS, earthquakes occurring between 0 and 70 kilometres are classified as shallow, those between 70 and 300 kilometres as intermediate, and those between 300 and 700 kilometres as deep earthquakes. The USGS further explains that the term "deep-focus earthquakes" is generally applied to earthquakes occurring at depths greater than 70 kilometres. It also notes that all earthquakes deeper than 70 kilometres are localised within great slabs of lithosphere that are sinking into the Earth's mantle. Explaining the relationship between earthquake depth and surface shaking, the USGS states that "the strength of shaking from an earthquake diminishes with increasing distance from the earthquake's source". It further observes that shaking at the surface from an earthquake occurring at 500 kilometres deep is considerably less than that from an earthquake of the same magnitude occurring at 20 kilometres depth. The USGS also states that earthquakes occur in the crust or upper mantle, which extends from the Earth's surface to about 800 kilometres. (ANI)

The earlier earthquake occurred at 4:42:28 pm IST at a depth of 183 kilometres, with its epicentre at latitude 36.548° North and longitude 70.951° East, according to the NCS. The NSC had reported the earlier event in another post on X, stating, "EQ of M: 3.9, On: 19/11/2026 16:42:28 IST, Lat: 36.548 N, Long: 70.951 E, Depth: 183 Km, Location: Afghanistan." It also notes that all earthquakes deeper than 70 kilometres are localised within great slabs of lithosphere that are sinking into the Earth's mantle. On the impact of earthquake depth on surface shaking, the USGS states that "the strength of shaking from an earthquake diminishes with increasing distance from the earthquake's source". It adds that shaking at the surface from an earthquake occurring at 500 kilometres deep is considerably less than that from an earthquake of the same magnitude occurring at 20 kilometres depth. According to the USGS, earthquakes occur in the crust or upper mantle, extending from the Earth's surface to depths of about 800 kilometres. (ANI)
